analysis.one_liner: Cuts the top corporate income tax rate from 35% to 30%.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, never received a hearing or a vote, and died when the 108th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Representative Mac Collins proposed lowering the highest corporate income tax rate on income over $75,000 to 30%, temporarily 32% for 2004-2006, down from 35%. Corporations with large profits would have paid billions less in federal taxes. The bill never advanced beyond its committee referral and expired at the end of the Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Large, profitable corporations would have paid a lower tax rate on income above $75,000, saving billions annually. Shareholders and executives would benefit from the higher after-tax profits.

how_it_helps.text: The bill cuts the top corporate rate on taxable income over $75,000 to 30%, down from 35%, with a temporary 32% rate for 2004, 2005, and 2006.
The reduction applies to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2003.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government would collect less corporate tax revenue, meaning the burden would fall on other taxpayers, on future borrowing, or on government programs that would otherwise be funded.

drawbacks.text: Lowering the top corporate rate would reduce federal revenue, shifting the cost onto individual taxpayers, deficits, or cuts elsewhere in the budget.
The cut only applies to income above $75,000, so corporations with modest profits would see little or no benefit while large corporations with big profits get the full reduction.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill directs a large, permanent tax cut to the most profitable corporations, including those paying record profits, while the revenue loss lands on everyone else. It contains no offsetting provisions, so an honest supporter would have to acknowledge it added to deficits or required raising taxes elsewhere.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on October 20, 2003 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
The committee took no further action, and the bill's only recorded history is introduction, sponsor remarks, and the committee referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal revenues were untouched; the general taxpayers and government programs that would have funded a large corporate tax cut are better off because the bill died without action.

for.name: Rep. Mac Collins
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled it for consideration; no hearing, markup, or vote ever occurred.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, and the bill drew no cosponsors from either party, so its support never took a measurable partisan shape.

industries.note: The bill would cut the top rate on corporate income over $75,000 from 35% to 30%, a direct revenue transfer to the most profitable firms. Their gain would come at the cost of federal revenue that otherwise funds programs or keeps other taxes lower.
